proposals.before: In the first year of Jianwu3 Guangwu obtained Gongsun Shu's treasure carriage; litters and palanquins were first complete.
proposals.after: In Jianwu year 13 Guangwu obtained Gongsun Shu's treasure carriage; litters and palanquins were first complete.
proposals.reason: Chinese 建武十三年 is Jianwu 13, not “first year of Jianwu3”; the literal mistranscribes the year.

proposals.before: Left Assistant Grandee Wang Xunzhi argued: "The great chariot was Yin’s sacrificial carriage, which is why it is absent from the Zhou chariot roster—yet the Hall of Brightness states, 'The great chariot is the Yin chariot.'
proposals.after: Left Assistant Grandee Wang Qunzhi argued: "The great chariot was Yin’s sacrificial carriage, which is why it is absent from the Zhou chariot roster—yet the Hall of Brightness states, 'The great chariot is the Yin chariot.'
proposals.reason: 逡之 is Qūnzhī; “Xunzhi” mismatches the Chinese given name 逡之.

proposals.before: Left Assistant Grandee Wang Xunzhi argued: "The great chariot was Yin’s sacrificial carriage; therefore it does not appear among the Zhou chariot names. Yet the Hall of Brightness says 'The great chariot is the Yin chariot.'
proposals.after: Left Assistant Grandee Wang Qunzhi argued: "The great chariot was Yin’s sacrificial carriage; therefore it does not appear among the Zhou chariot names. Yet the Hall of Brightness says 'The great chariot is the Yin chariot.'
proposals.reason: 逡之 is Qūnzhī; the literal likewise wrongly romanizes 逡 as Xun.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Jin granted the Prince of Anping, Xian, Fu, a mica palanquin.
proposals.after: Emperor Wu of Jin granted Prince Xian of Anping, Fu, a mica palanquin.
proposals.reason: Literal “Prince of Anping, Xian, Fu” splits the posthumous title 獻 and personal name 孚 confusingly.

proposals.before: Princes of the five grades and martial officials did not wear them; only when also serving as palace attendants did they do so.
proposals.after: Princes and dukes of the five grades and martial officials did not wear them; only when also serving as palace attendants did they do so.
proposals.reason: Chinese 王公五等 includes both princes (王) and dukes (公); the idiomatic English omits dukes.

proposals.before: Princes of the five grades and martial officials did not wear them; only with added palace attendant status did they wear them.
proposals.after: Princes and dukes of the five grades and martial officials did not wear them; only with added palace attendant status did they wear them.
proposals.reason: Chinese 王公五等 includes both princes (王) and dukes (公); the literal English omits dukes.

proposals.before: In the fourth year of Jianyuan it was ordered that princes, marquises, ministers, and chief administrators use pearl and rock crystal; all others ivory and tridacna.
proposals.after: In the fourth year of Jianyuan it was ordered that princes, dukes, marquises, ministers, and chief administrators use pearl and rock crystal; all others ivory and tridacna.
proposals.reason: Chinese 王公侯卿尹 lists 公 (dukes) after princes; the idiomatic English skips dukes.

proposals.before: In the fourth year of Jianyuan, a regulation fixed that princes, marquises, ministers, and chief administrators used pearl and rock crystal; the rest used ivory and tridacna.
proposals.after: In the fourth year of Jianyuan, a regulation fixed that princes, dukes, marquises, ministers, and chief administrators used pearl and rock crystal; the rest used ivory and tridacna.
proposals.reason: Chinese 王公侯卿尹 lists 公 (dukes) after princes; the literal English skips dukes.

decisions.reason: Chinese 建武十三年 is Jianwu year 13; “first year of Jianwu3” misreads 十三 as a garbled era form. The proposed literal restores the correct year without changing the rest.
王逡之 has given name 逡之, romanized Qūnzhī; Xunzhi wrongly reads 逡 as Xun. Replacing with Wang Qunzhi corrects the name while preserving the memorial wording.
The same 王逡之 appears in the literal; Qunzhi is the correct romanization of 逡之, and the proposed change fixes only that naming error.

安平獻王孚 is Prince Xian of Anping, personal name Fu; splitting 獻 as a bare “Xian” after “Prince of Anping” confuses posthumous title with personal name. “Prince Xian of Anping, Fu” restores the standard title-plus-name reading.
王公五等 names both 王 (princes) and 公 (dukes) among the five-grade nobility; the original idiomatic omits dukes, and inserting “and dukes” restores that referent.
The literal likewise renders 王公五等 as princes only; adding dukes recovers 公 without otherwise altering the sentence.
建元四年…王公侯卿尹 lists 公 after 王; the idiomatic skips dukes between princes and marquises, and the proposal restores that rank.
The same 王公侯卿尹 sequence requires dukes in the literal; adding “dukes” after princes corrects the omission.
